Straight to the point, Team: The Electoral College is an outdated mess that political parties are using to game the system and perpetuate power for candidates who get less votes. It's simply a tool to use land mass as inflated power instead of the will of the people.
Momentum is growing to end this shady scheme once and for all but we need your help to get over the top. Support our work with $25 or more right now to relegate it to the dustbin of history >> [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-end-electoral-college?refcode=060926_2&amount=25]
Voter Action Project [https://voteractionproject.org/]
Fox News: End of the Electoral College is in sight if Democrats keep getting their way [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-end-electoral-college?refcode=060926_2&amount=25]
Fox News is wrong, friend -- big surprise.
Our movement to end the Electoral College isn't about partisanship. It's not about gaming the system. Fox has spent decades drowning in their own rhetoric and can't understand the simple fact of people choosing a system that's right and just over a system that benefits themselves and silences others.
Fox News is worried about political parties. We're worried about the people's voices being heard and their votes meaning something . We're worried about a system that has rewarded the popular vote loser with the job anyway five times now. We're worried about the people and the states that get ignored and lost along the way to *just enough* Electoral College votes.
The Electoral College is an antiquated system built for a vastly different America and can't stand up to the challenges we face today. RUSH $25 or whatever you can today to help end it forever >> [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-end-electoral-college?refcode=060926_2&amount=25]

| | Never let anyone tell you that these fights aren’t winnable. Of course, we have our work cut out for us. We’ve seen outrageous attacks on multiracial democracy in the past several weeks, including new rigged voting maps that silence voters of color. But we’ve also seen a movement rising up to fight back. And we’ve seen that new gerrymanders aren’t inevitable, even though extremists want you to think they are. **South Carolina lawmakers failed to pass new voting maps** that would have eliminated their only congressional district where Black voters are free to elect the candidates of their choice. **Georgians broke early-vote records** with over a million ballots cast before May’s elections, showing that people are fired up to take ownership over our democracy. Democrats’ early turnout surged by 54% compared to the same point four years ago. **Across the South, this movement has helped drive grassroots organizing** since the Supreme Court’s ruling in _Callais_ — with an estimated **1 million+ contacts to voters** across Georgia, Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Tennessee these last few weeks to oppose new rigged maps. That’s exactly the type of mobilization we need to stop additional gerrymanders in the short term and build a more robust, more representative democracy in the long term. This month, we’re rallying Georgians to oppose new rigged maps in a special redistricting session that Governor Brian Kemp just called. And for years to come, we’ll keep fighting for fair representation and the freedom to vote — to stop new attempts at voter suppression, and to pass new, affirmative voting rights protections at the state and federal level. When we suit up, come together, and fight for a democracy where everyone’s voice gets heard, we can make real change.

clean_body: Don’t believe the cynics | | | Never let anyone tell you that these fights aren’t winnable. Of course, we have our work cut out for us. We’ve seen outrageous attacks on multiracial democracy in the past several weeks, including new rigged voting maps that silence voters of color. But we’ve also seen a movement rising up to fight back. And we’ve seen that new gerrymanders aren’t inevitable, even though extremists want you to think they are. South Carolina lawmakers failed to pass new voting maps that would have eliminated their only congressional district where Black voters are free to elect the candidates of their choice. Georgians broke early-vote records with over a million ballots cast before May’s elections, showing that people are fired up to take ownership over our democracy. Democrats’ early turnout surged by 54% compared to the same point four years ago. Across the South, this movement has helped drive grassroots organizing since the Supreme Court’s ruling in Callais — with an estimated 1 million+ contacts to voters across Georgia, Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Tennessee these last few weeks to oppose new rigged maps. That’s exactly the type of mobilization we need to stop additional gerrymanders in the short term and build a more robust, more representative democracy in the long term. This month, we’re rallying Georgians to oppose new rigged maps in a special redistricting session that Governor Brian Kemp just called. And for years to come, we’ll keep fighting for fair representation and the freedom to vote — to stop new attempts at voter suppression, and to pass new, affirmative voting rights protections at the state and federal level. | | |

Friend, Deb Haaland here — did you catch _Morning Joe_ this morning? I joined to talk about why governors matter now more than ever and why I’m ready to lead New Mexico in this moment:

...Leadership is important in our country. And certainly, governor[s are] the first line of defense against the worst policies coming out of the Trump administration.”**

We need leadership that knows how to stand up to the Trump administration, fight back against dangerous policies coming out of Washington, and deliver real results for New Mexicans.

Let me be honest with you about something.
I'm not supposed to be in this race.
The grandson of a sharecropper? Not supposed to be a viable Senate candidate in Louisiana.
A Black farmer from rural Tensas Parish? Not supposed to compete statewide in the Deep South.
Someone without billionaire backers or a Rolodex full of Washington insiders? Not supposed to have a shot at flipping a Senate seat.
But here we are.
And MAGA is absolutely shocked.
They thought Louisiana was locked up. They thought they could focus on defending seats in swing states while the South stayed safely red. They thought a race like ours — a real populist challenge to their grip on power — wasn't possible here.
They were wrong.
Look at what's happening: Democrats flipping Trump districts across the South. MAGA candidates tearing each other apart in primaries. Republican retirements at levels not seen since the Great Depression. Trump's approval cratering over his failed Iran war.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opening. The kind of moment that doesn't come around often in Louisiana politics.
And I believe — deep in my bones — that this is the campaign to meet this moment.
Not because I'm the most polished politician. Not because I've been planning a Senate run my whole career. But because I understand what working Louisianans need because I've lived their struggles.
I know what it's like to watch costs rise while your income stays flat. I know what it's like to compete against corporations that rig the system against family operations. I know what it's like to worry about whether there will be anything left for the next generation.
That's the authentic economic populism that can win here. Not the fake MAGA version that delivers nothing but culture wars — the real thing that actually fights for working people.
And if we capitalize on this moment — if we show the political world that Louisiana is genuinely winnable — everything changes.
Not just for this race. For the entire map. For what's possible in the South.
But only if we have the resources to compete. And that counts on good folks like you stepping up.
Will you chip in $50, $25, or $10 to help us seize this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity? [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rrr-jamie]
CHIP IN TO FLIP THIS SENATE SEAT! >> [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rrr-jamie]
We have the opportunity to pull off something historic in Louisiana that will do a whole lot of good for people here. I couldn’t be more grateful to have you fighting alongside me.
Jamie Davis

**Pride Month is in full swing. Millions of LGBTQIA+ Americans are celebrating who they are and living as their authentic selves out loud.**

But Trump and his MAGA Republican allies continue to take our fundamental freedoms away. Here are some examples:

1️⃣→ Trump’s hand-picked justices on the Supreme Court **banned gender-affirming care** and **are allowing for civil protections to be taken away** for trans kids and adults.

1️⃣→ They’re **fighting to allow discrimination against the LGBTQIA+ community** and are rebranding June as “**Nuclear Family Month.”**

1️⃣→ And right now, **MAGA Republicans want to suppress our right to vote under the Save America Act.**

[For far too long, we’ve watched Trump and his MAGA cronies distract from their agenda of erasing our community. But not anymore, friend. Will you stand with the Voter Protection Project and fight to elect Democrats who stand with the LGBTQIA+ community by donating $5 now?](https://act.protectvoting.org/go/112101?t=7&akid=25021%2E878179%2EecNz5e) | [DONATE $5 TO PROTECT LGBTQIA+ AMERICANS »](https://act.protectvoting.org/go/112101?t=8&akid=25021%2E878179%2EecNz5e)

This fight is one we must win, folks. But to win, all of us need to stand up to Trump’s agenda of bigotry and hate.

When our side shows up online, we shape the narrative heading into the final days of early voting.

**Step 2: Make your plan to vote early by June 12**

Early Voting is already underway and runs through Friday, June 12 then the Runoff Election Day is Tuesday, June 16.

Don’t wait until the last minute. Make a plan:

* Check your voting location and hours here:[ https://swampthevoteusa.com/georgia](http://links.burtjonesforga.com/u/click?_t=858b83d5086141569cc77db3b7b1b605&_m=9079323b62a44e9abd10ffe11b2a4e93&_e=m0-Whm7P9bh-cWAAiz7nCwWmPLoGRP8KIlQaFwVq0G_yWwyYDgQNr6YnQ5HUIUq3W4FYEeu5rWa3AaYWFNclKyduK02bBaOmGHQ6niwE-z-hTSGFWLFNfG5IAoS1cQb2RzwXCf1egcvjbLaVZDlwwAUQWUOtmMF1Op-k2j2faDXjPHMz-1eilxpqKVUzgqF7ftDoVEHhcOR4TZDoM6f2VMBOBgToYGMJC--ieYspozoFFMowItzqB1R6eMlYWWgqgOzjV5ghcFo6rHAeq_mAL6XT3q_-UciOf2HcFyy290oAdAeKKAv0IwTAe0PHzGprTu_DdWCcoErhqtzIoTn8fw%3D%3D)
* Decide which day you’re voting early: between now and Friday, June 12.
* Bring a valid photo ID and remind at least one friend to go with you.

**Step 3: Turn your support into votes**

After you share President Trump’s post and lock in your own voting plan, help us expand the map:

* Call or text 10 like‐minded friends and ask: “Have you seen President Trump’s endorsement of Burt Jones? Have you voted yet?”
* Share the Swamp The Vote link with them so they can find their own voting location:[ https://swampthevoteusa.com/georgia/](http://links.burtjonesforga.com/u/click?_t=858b83d5086141569cc77db3b7b1b605&_m=9079323b62a44e9abd10ffe11b2a4e93&_e=m0-Whm7P9bh-cWAAiz7nCwWmPLoGRP8KIlQaFwVq0G9kPO6gMVu7MwBy-zy8detTMSIPPXV079PNbuxY0xhRYZH2uSx48YcJLqLzmvmZHzvpUAmxdufx4f-NT3M5KnnqMDLG4psoo1Oim9wnOuiO4KSoMH7D7GvSZ9yZya-DiUwHVErKYWQdW3Hw6_P34UTlTPp6NFjdm3lzmWsZI0MJCMHzcqpuuGGeTFCOkbZOOtcZjy1UardtqYrCOb4bF8I-xdNHR4gTT8VXIbyCkgB6ulxbRZPQ6fUK6HQ9UGdUKjJQ6rvefUru-zJI5iQNtmwBGxJyVbJA1dGJoqqgPRr40g%3D%3D)
* Post a quick selfie or photo online after you vote with the caption: “I voted for Burt Jones – President Trump’s choice for Georgia Governor. Early voting through June 12, Election Day June 16.”

Every conversation, every share, and every early vote helps us send a clear message: Georgia is Trump Country, and we’re all in for Burt Jones.

Thank you for standing with President Trump and Burt Jones in this critical moment for our state.

Let’s swamp the vote and finish strong.

– Team Burt Jones for Governor

body:
I’m honored to be your Democratic nominee for Nevada governor.
# [](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/12?t=1&akid=268%2E127862%2EmO2q67)
Friends,
Tonight, Nevada Democrats made me their nominee for governor.
I want to be honest with you about what I'm feeling right now: **grateful, fired up, and ready to work.**
**[If you’re ready to flip Nevada blue this November, then I’m humbly asking you to donate to our campaign today. This is a toss-up race, and we’re going to need every bit of support to win.](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/1?c0=em_ms_af_20260609_2_ak.GfrSEh&amount=5&refcode=em20260609-263&t=2&akid=268%2E127862%2EmO2q67)**
**[Donate $5 ››](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/1?c0=em_ms_af_20260609_2_ak.GfrSEh&amount=5&refcode=em20260609-263&t=21&akid=268%2E127862%2EmO2q67)**
This is a campaign for the entirety of the Nevada family. Here’s what I mean by that:
**No one should have to struggle to find a good-paying job, pay their bills, afford healthcare, or raise a family in our state — but under the Lombardo-Trump economy, Nevadans are _worse off_ than they were years before.**
We need someone in the governor’s office who knows what it’s like to rely on food stamps, WIC, and Medicaid.
We also need someone who won’t turn their backs on working people to please mega corporations and Donald Trump.
I’ve lived through that struggle and know how important it is for people to have a government that truly invests in them — and I promise you, I’ll never forget that.
But we won’t win this race on values alone. The MAGA money machine is already working overtime to protect Governor Joe Lombardo, and the only way we’ll compete with their multi-million dollar war chest is if we band together.
The latest polling shows I’m statistically tied with Lombardo. **This race is winnable, but it can easily slip away from us if we sit back and wait.**
**[So please, make a $5 contribution now to help us flip Nevada blue:](https://act.fordfornevada.com/go/1?c0=em_ms_af_20260609_2_ak.GfrSEh&amount=5&refcode=em20260609-263&t=22&akid=268%2E127862%2EmO2q67)**

Thanks so much,
Aaron

Before the 1970s, American voters had a reasonable claim on three protections against political capture.
* The first was a meaningful limit on how much money any person, corporation, or union could spend influencing an election.
* The second was a federal court system willing to intervene when state legislatures drew maps designed to silence voters.
* The third was a body of voting rights law that could stop maps designed to dilute the political power of Black voters and other voters of color.

Today, voters have none of these protections in federal court.
Each was removed by the United States Supreme Court -- by specific cases, decided by specific majorities, over warning dissents. The cases span fifty years. Together they form the legal architecture of the rigged map: the doctrinal scaffolding that lets money flow into politics without limit, and lets gerrymandered maps stand without remedy.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/6da3ef34-2681-49d2-8963-b017f6639c3c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

United States Supreme Court
[The story we told in Part 1 -- REDMAP, PA-7](https://substack.com/redirect/a2d577ab-b17e-45e1-8fdb-d14d07e2a7c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), the closed-door drawing of district lines for the 2010s -- happened inside this legal architecture. The four rulings are not the prequel to REDMAP. They are its precondition and its protection -- though whether each was intended to enable what it later did is a different answer in each case. _Buckley_ in 1976 was decided on a sincere free-speech theory by a cross-ideological coalition. _Citizens United_ in 2010 was decided over a 90-page dissent that warned in detail of the corporate domination that did in fact follow. _Rucho_ and _Callais_ , more recently, were decided over dissents that named the political consequences and were ignored. The legal story and the operational story are one story, told from two angles.
* * *
## [The Rigged Map --Part 1: How They Drew the Map](https://substack.com/redirect/59779cb5-6c0c-46d4-924c-acb2f0922403?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

[Before 2011, Pennsylvania's 7th congressional district was a place where elections actually mattered. The district covered most of Delaware County, the Philadelphia suburbs west and south of the city. From the mid-1970s through the late 1980s it elected a Democrat; from then through the mid-2000s, a Republican, Curt Weldon. In 2006, Navy vice admiral Jo...](https://substack.com/redirect/59779cb5-6c0c-46d4-924c-acb2f0922403?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

* * *
Each ruling came from a Republican-appointed majority. The first was issued by a court Nixon had largely built -- four of his appointees sat on the bench that struck down the post-Watergate reforms Congress had passed in response to Nixon's own campaign-finance abuses. The most recent came from a six-justice conservative majority, the product of a fifty-year Federalist Society project to capture the federal judiciary. The dissenters in every case were Democratic appointees, and they were always outnumbered.
* * *
## _[Buckley v. Valeo](https://substack.com/redirect/1b441ca4-4875-4dbe-bea7-cb40ef9f4832?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[ (1976)](https://substack.com/redirect/1b441ca4-4875-4dbe-bea7-cb40ef9f4832?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d2f0f7f3-918f-4a7a-96c8-5049cb7d3ddb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[https://www.ifs.org/blog/reflecting-on-50-years-of-buckley-v-valeo/](https://substack.com/redirect/a8332284-b594-4bbc-b511-3aa174748027?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
In the years after Watergate, Congress passed the most ambitious campaign finance law in American history. The Federal Election Campaign Act, as amended in 1974, capped what individuals could give to candidates, what candidates could spend on themselves, what outside groups could spend independently, and what campaigns could spend overall. The post-Watergate consensus was that the right to free speech did not include a right to drown out other people's speech.
In 1976, in _[Buckley v. Valeo](https://substack.com/redirect/1b441ca4-4875-4dbe-bea7-cb40ef9f4832?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ , the Supreme Court ruled that consensus was wrong.
The case was decided per curiam by a six-to-two Republican-appointed bench. The justices upheld FECA's contribution limits but struck down every other cap -- on candidate self-financing, on overall campaign spending, on independent expenditures by outside groups. Spending money to communicate political ideas, the Court ruled, was itself protected First Amendment speech, and speech could not be limited just because some speakers had more of it than others.
The shorthand -- "money is speech" -- overstates the holding but captures the result. Before _Buckley_ , money in politics was a regulated activity. After _Buckley_ , it was a constitutional right. Every subsequent campaign finance decision rests on this foundation.
_Buckley_ did not arrive as a corporate project. The lead plaintiff was Senator James Buckley, a Conservative from New York, joined by former Senator Eugene McCarthy, the Democrat whose 1968 anti-war insurgency had driven Lyndon Johnson out of the presidential race.
[The American Civil Liberties Union](https://substack.com/redirect/d4cb3a2a-ad2c-4680-a5d5-bcb2e3ade8dd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was a plaintiff, and its lawyer Joel Gora argued the case. The coalition's argument was that FECA was an incumbents' protection act: capping campaign spending froze the playing field in favor of officeholders with built-in name recognition, and outsider candidates needed to raise and spend big money to be heard.
Both Buckley and McCarthy had built insurgent campaigns on large seed-money contributions FECA would have made illegal -- and both said they could not have done so under the new law.
The doctrine they argued, political spending is political speech, and cannot be capped was, in 1976, a populist argument. Districts were broadly competitive, outside spending was modest, and capping spending in those conditions did freeze the playing field against insurgent challengers.
That system has since been deliberately dismantled by gerrymandering that took away district competitiveness. Also, by the unlimited outside spending _Buckley_ and its successors made possible. The doctrine designed to liberate outsiders from incumbent protection became, in time, the doctrine that built a different and more durable kind of incumbent protection.
_Buckley_ 's ACLU lawyers in 1976 imagined a world where Eugene McCarthy could raise seed money from a handful of supporters and challenge a sitting president. The world _Buckley_ helped produce is one where McCarthy could raise that money, but no district would be competitive enough for it to matter, and no primary safe from the PAC money that would arrive to defend the establishment. The terms of the trade have flipped.
_Buckley_ 's architects did not intend this. Their foresight was limited; the rulings that followed did not share that limitation.
* * *
## _[Citizens United v. FEC](https://substack.com/redirect/b6e90b3d-72dd-46e9-8907-e58dee3d0a9b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[ ](https://substack.com/redirect/b6e90b3d-72dd-46e9-8907-e58dee3d0a9b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)(2010)
By the early 2000s, billions of dollars in corporate and union treasury funds were available to influence elections, if a legal route opened. The 2002 Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act -- McCain-Feingold -- barred corporations and unions from using treasury funds for political ads naming a candidate in the weeks before an election. The premise was that a single CEO should not outspend an entire grassroots operation in the final stretch.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/cd49b594-3a89-4018-964f-50055881f6e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
In 2010, in _Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission_ , a 5-4 majority struck down the corporate spending restriction entirely.
The plaintiff was a conservative nonprofit that had produced a documentary critical of Hillary Clinton during the 2008 primary; broadcasting the film close to the primary was illegal under [McCain-Feingold](https://substack.com/redirect/bd567e9e-c113-4b84-9ba8-1d78795503c3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/ba120dbe-7827-4dcc-9d3f-f5627d750a2c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[John McCain](https://substack.com/redirect/bf5cf447-b495-4600-8877-b21860e39d36?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) (R-AZ) and [Russ Feingold](https://substack.com/redirect/2b4c5e18-25b7-49bf-b71e-8cf998c5990e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) (D-WI)
The Court could have ruled narrowly. Instead, Justice Kennedy's majority opinion declared that the government had no constitutional authority to limit independent political spending by corporations or unions at all. Corporations, the Court ruled, possess First Amendment political-speech rights essentially identical to those of individual citizens.
The final opinion bore Kennedy's name, but the broader ruling was, by most credible reconstructions of the Court's internal deliberations, Roberts's project. He withdrew his own narrower opinion to let Kennedy's expansive draft become the majority, then orchestrated a reargument that gave the eventual ruling a clean procedural record on broad constitutional questions the parties had not originally briefed.
This was not a ruling that produced unforeseen consequences. Justice Stevens wrote a ninety-page dissent, joined by Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor, that anticipated in detail the corporate domination of electioneering that did in fact follow. An earlier dissent draft by Justice Souter -- circulated within the Court but later withdrawn -- accused the majority of having manipulated Court procedures to reach an expansive result on issues neither party had raised. Four justices saw what was coming. Five chose to proceed anyway.
Within months, a federal appeals court ruling -- _[SpeechNow.org v. FEC](https://substack.com/redirect/54899d94-2ce1-42be-a3f7-9d0ef1074bb0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ -- extended _Citizens United_ to political action committees, giving birth to the super PAC: unlimited fundraising and spending, conditional on a non-coordination requirement that turned out to be largely theoretical.
The effect was immediate and durable. In 2008, the last cycle before _Citizens United_ , outside groups spent roughly $338 million on federal elections; by 2024, more than $4.5 billion. Most flows through 501(c)(4) "social welfare" organizations that need not disclose donors. Money once raised in capped contributions from named individuals now flows in unlimited sums from sources voters cannot see -- to candidates of both parties.
* * *
## _[Rucho v. Common Cause](https://substack.com/redirect/e1ce2801-ed32-4562-a749-e5bb6a92a684?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ (2019)
For decades after _Buckley_ , voters challenging gerrymandered maps had at least a theoretical federal-court path. When a legislature drew lines specifically to entrench one party's power regardless of how voters voted, the maps violated the Equal Protection Clause and the First Amendment's guarantee of meaningful political association. Lower federal courts had developed workable standards for distinguishing extreme partisan gerrymanders from ordinary political map-drawing. The Supreme Court had indicated that, with such a standard, federal judges could step in.
In 2019, in _Rucho v. Common Cause_ , the Court ruled that no such standard existed and never would.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8de2d5d9-6e28-470d-be3d-1d4680f4ac7f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The case combined a Republican gerrymander in North Carolina, designed to lock in a 10-3 congressional advantage in a 50-50 state, with a Democratic gerrymander in Maryland, designed to flip a long-held Republican seat. Both parties had gerrymandered; both sets of plaintiffs argued the maps violated the Constitution. Chief Justice Roberts's 5-4 majority opinion held that partisan gerrymandering claims presented _" political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts."_
This was a chosen result, not a forced one. Lower federal courts had been developing the very standards Roberts's opinion claimed could not exist. Justice Kagan's dissent named what the majority was doing: _" For the first time ever, this Court refuses to remedy a constitutional violation because it thinks the task beyond judicial capabilities."_ The "first time ever" is the operative phrase. The Court did not lack the tools. It declined to use them.
_Rucho_ closed the federal courthouse to every voter, in every state, who believed their map had been drawn to silence them. North Carolina's gerrymander stood. Maryland's gerrymander stood.
So did Wisconsin's, where the Republican gerrymander produced a 64-35 GOP supermajority in the State Assembly in a state that votes near 50-50 in statewide races. So did Texas's.
So did Florida's. So did Tennessee's, where the 2022 Republican-drawn congressional map split Nashville across three districts to dilute its Democratic majority, shifting the state's delegation from 7-2 Republican to 8-1.
So did Ohio's, where the state Supreme Court struck down the Republican-drawn maps as unconstitutional partisan gerrymanders and was ignored by Republican map drawers who used the rejected maps anyway.
The only path left for voters facing a rigged map was state court under a state constitution, decided by a state supreme court, in one of the small number of states where that path even exists.
[It was the path Pennsylvania took, in 2018, to undo the PA-7 gerrymander we traced in Part 1.](https://substack.com/redirect/a2d577ab-b17e-45e1-8fdb-d14d07e2a7c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

## _[Louisiana v. Callais](https://substack.com/redirect/99d7d782-f908-4016-abac-ef52a7a1bc86?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ (2026)
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/339a74b6-0f5b-403e-a0d7-85fed30c12f9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[LWV: In this map, districts 2 and 6 (the lime green and pink districts) are majority Black districts](https://substack.com/redirect/b9c57bdc-ddc4-4f48-9026-e462195c0456?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
For sixty years, voters of color had one tool federal courts could not refuse: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Where state legislatures drew maps that diluted the political power of Black, Latino, or Asian American voters -- packing them into one district to waste their votes, or splitting them across many to neutralize them -- Section 2 let those voters sue in federal court. The provision had been used successfully in Alabama, Louisiana, Georgia, Mississippi, Texas, and dozens of other states. As recently as 2023, the Roberts Court had reaffirmed Section 2 in _Allen v. Milligan_ , ruling for Black voters in Alabama.
Three years later, on April 29, 2026, in _[Louisiana v. Callais](https://substack.com/redirect/99d7d782-f908-4016-abac-ef52a7a1bc86?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ , the Court reversed course.
The case was about a Louisiana congressional map that contained a second majority-Black district, drawn under a prior federal court order. A group of "non-Black voters" challenged the map, arguing the Black-opportunity district itself constituted unconstitutional racial discrimination. Justice Alito's 6-3 majority opinion agreed and narrowed Section 2 so dramatically that Justice Kagan, in dissent, wrote that the provision was now _" all but a dead letter."_
The Court did not formally overturn Section 2. It made it functionally unenforceable through three doctrinal changes: plaintiffs must submit sample maps meeting all of a state's political objectives, must disentangle racial bloc voting from ordinary partisan preference, and must prove "present-day intentional racial discrimination" -- with historical patterns entitled to "much less weight." Each requirement is plausible alone. Together, they raise the bar so high that most cases that succeeded under Section 2 over forty years would now fail.
Of the four rulings, _Callais_ is the one whose consequences were not just foreseen but procedurally facilitated. The Court finalized its judgment in five days instead of the standard thirty-two, allowing states to redraw maps before the 2026 elections. Louisiana suspended its May 16 primary mid-election. Alabama filed an emergency motion the day after the ruling, asking the Court to reinstate the very maps it had struck down three years earlier. Analysts have estimated that up to a quarter of the Congressional Black Caucus could lose their seats to map redrawing in years ahead. The reversal of _Allen v. Milligan_ after only three years, the doctrinal changes designed to make Section 2 unenforceable, and the compressed schedule -- none of these was accidental.
* * *
## What's Left
Fifty years after _Buckley_ , the legal protections American voters once had against political capture have been systematically removed. Money in politics cannot be capped. Partisan gerrymandering cannot be challenged in federal court. Racial vote dilution can no longer be effectively challenged either.
The doctrine Senator Buckley and his coalition argued for in 1976 -- that free political spending would liberate outsider voices against entrenched incumbent power -- has produced its inversion. Outside spending is free, but the voices it amplifies belong overwhelmingly to interests far better resourced than any insurgent candidate. The conditions that made _Buckley_ 's argument plausible have been destroyed by the legal architecture the doctrine made possible. The 1976 trade was sincere. It was not what it appeared to be. After 1976, the warnings became more specific; by 2026, dissents described the consequences in operational detail. The majorities proceeded anyway.
What remains is the state court path Pennsylvania used to undo PA-7: a state constitution, a willing state supreme court, and a political coalition capable of building and sustaining that court's majority. That path exists in roughly a dozen states. It is itself under sustained, well-funded attack -- by the same actors who built the strategy that produced PA-7 in the first place.
**In Part 3, we follow where the money has gone, and what it has bought.**

Money once raised in capped contributions from named individuals now flows in unlimited sums from sources voters cannot see -- to candidates of both parties. (2019) For decades after Buckley , voters challenging gerrymandered maps had at least a theoretical federal-court path. When a legislature drew lines specifically to entrench one party's power regardless of how voters voted, the maps violated the Equal Protection Clause and the First Amendment's guarantee of meaningful political association. Lower federal courts had developed workable standards for distinguishing extreme partisan gerrymanders from ordinary political map-drawing. The Supreme Court had indicated that, with such a standard, federal judges could step in. In 2019, in Rucho v. Common Cause , the Court ruled that no such standard existed and never would. | | ---|---|--- The case combined a Republican gerrymander in North Carolina, designed to lock in a 10-3 congressional advantage in a 50-50 state, with a Democratic gerrymander in Maryland, designed to flip a long-held Republican seat. Both parties had gerrymandered; both sets of plaintiffs argued the maps violated the Constitution. Chief Justice Roberts's 5-4 majority opinion held that partisan gerrymandering claims presented " political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts." This was a chosen result, not a forced one. Lower federal courts had been developing the very standards Roberts's opinion claimed could not exist. Justice Kagan's dissent named what the majority was doing: " For the first time ever, this Court refuses to remedy a constitutional violation because it thinks the task beyond judicial capabilities." The "first time ever" is the operative phrase. The Court did not lack the tools. It declined to use them. Rucho closed the federal courthouse to every voter, in every state, who believed their map had been drawn to silence them. North Carolina's gerrymander stood. Maryland's gerrymander stood. So did Wisconsin's, where the Republican gerrymander produced a 64-35 GOP supermajority in the State Assembly in a state that votes near 50-50 in statewide races. So did Texas's. So did Florida's. So did Tennessee's, where the 2022 Republican-drawn congressional map split Nashville across three districts to dilute its Democratic majority, shifting the state's delegation from 7-2 Republican to 8-1. So did Ohio's, where the state Supreme Court struck down the Republican-drawn maps as unconstitutional partisan gerrymanders and was ignored by Republican map drawers who used the rejected maps anyway. The only path left for voters facing a rigged map was state court under a state constitution, decided by a state supreme court, in one of the small number of states where that path even exists. | | and | | ---|---|--- | May 12 | (2026) | | ---|---|--- For sixty years, voters of color had one tool federal courts could not refuse: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Where state legislatures drew maps that diluted the political power of Black, Latino, or Asian American voters -- packing them into one district to waste their votes, or splitting them across many to neutralize them -- Section 2 let those voters sue in federal court. The provision had been used successfully in Alabama, Louisiana, Georgia, Mississippi, Texas, and dozens of other states. As recently as 2023, the Roberts Court had reaffirmed Section 2 in Allen v. Milligan , ruling for Black voters in Alabama. Three years later, on April 29, 2026, in , the Court reversed course. The case was about a Louisiana congressional map that contained a second majority-Black district, drawn under a prior federal court order. A group of "non-Black voters" challenged the map, arguing the Black-opportunity district itself constituted unconstitutional racial discrimination. Justice Alito's 6-3 majority opinion agreed and narrowed Section 2 so dramatically that Justice Kagan, in dissent, wrote that the provision was now " all but a dead letter." The Court did not formally overturn Section 2. It made it functionally unenforceable through three doctrinal changes: plaintiffs must submit sample maps meeting all of a state's political objectives, must disentangle racial bloc voting from ordinary partisan preference, and must prove "present-day intentional racial discrimination" -- with historical patterns entitled to "much less weight." Each requirement is plausible alone. Together, they raise the bar so high that most cases that succeeded under Section 2 over forty years would now fail. Of the four rulings, Callais is the one whose consequences were not just foreseen but procedurally facilitated. The Court finalized its judgment in five days instead of the standard thirty-two, allowing states to redraw maps before the 2026 elections. Louisiana suspended its May 16 primary mid-election. Alabama filed an emergency motion the day after the ruling, asking the Court to reinstate the very maps it had struck down three years earlier. Analysts have estimated that up to a quarter of the Congressional Black Caucus could lose their seats to map redrawing in years ahead. The reversal of Allen v. Milligan after only three years, the doctrinal changes designed to make Section 2 unenforceable, and the compressed schedule -- none of these was accidental. What's Left Fifty years after Buckley , the legal protections American voters once had against political capture have been systematically removed. Money in politics cannot be capped. Partisan gerrymandering cannot be challenged in federal court. Racial vote dilution can no longer be effectively challenged either. The doctrine Senator Buckley and his coalition argued for in 1976 -- that free political spending would liberate outsider voices against entrenched incumbent power -- has produced its inversion. Outside spending is free, but the voices it amplifies belong overwhelmingly to interests far better resourced than any insurgent candidate. The conditions that made Buckley 's argument plausible have been destroyed by the legal architecture the doctrine made possible. The 1976 trade was sincere. It was not what it appeared to be. After 1976, the warnings became more specific; by 2026, dissents described the consequences in operational detail. The majorities proceeded anyway. What remains is the state court path Pennsylvania used to undo PA-7: a state constitution, a willing state supreme court, and a political coalition capable of building and sustaining that court's majority. That path exists in roughly a dozen states. It is itself under sustained, well-funded attack -- by the same actors who built the strategy that produced PA-7 in the first place. In Part 3, we follow where the money has gone, and what it has bought. Stay Angry Sources -- The Rigged Map: Part 2 1. Buckley v. Valeo , 424 U.S. 1 (1976). Per curiam decision of the U.S. Supreme Court. 2. Joel Gora, "Celebrating Buckley v. Valeo : A Landmark of Political Freedom," Institute for Free Speech, January 2026. Retrospective by the ACLU lawyer who argued Buckley. 3. Brooklyn Law School. "Professor Joel Gora Looks Back at His Role in Supreme Court Case Buckley v. Valeo 50 Years Later." January 30, 2026. 4. Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission , 558 U.S. 310 (2010). Majority opinion by Justice Anthony Kennedy; dissent by Justice John Paul Stevens, joined by Justices Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor. 5. SpeechNow.org v. Federal Election Commission , 599 F.3d 686 (D.C. Cir. 2010). 6. Rucho v. Common Cause , 588 U.S. 684 (2019). name: State Representative Ryan Chamberlin
subject: Budget and Property Tax Relief - PASSED!
body:
Newsletter from Rep. Ryan Chamberlin

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/repryanchamberlin/newsletter-from-rep-ryan-chamberlin-kqs1grv7ud-12934252?e=d1c1b9864f)
---
| | | | |
---
| |
# NEWSLETTER FROM REP. RYAN CHAMBERLIN
---
| | Friends and Neighbors,
The past two weeks have been especially important in Tallahassee as we **passed Florida’s state budget** and **returned for a special session focused on property tax relief.** The budget now awaits the Governor’s approval, and I was proud to support efforts that continue to keep Florida fiscally strong. **Perhaps the biggest news is that property tax relief is now heading to the ballot.** That’s not the finish line — that’s the starting gun. The road to total elimination of property taxes for homeowners begins right here, right now. First steps are the hardest. Good thing we didn’t come here to take the easy ones. Time to work.
As always, please do not hesitate to [**contact my office**](https://ryanchamberlin.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=ec15c6093052c02efbd22b6cd&id=2e6ab9efb5&e=d1c1b9864f) if there is something we can do for you. My team and I would be more than happy to help you in any way we can.
---
| |
# Florida Property Tax Reform
---
|
---
| | The **Florida Legislature passed two bills** aimed at **providing property tax relief** for homeowners and **strengthening homestead protections.**
**WHAT PASSED:**
* [**CS/HJR 1F – Constitutional Amendment:**](https://ryanchamberlin.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=ec15c6093052c02efbd22b6cd&id=a19af0f0b8&e=d1c1b9864f)Places the proposal on the 2026 ballot for Florida voters.
* [**CS/HB 3F – Implementation Bill:**](https://ryanchamberlin.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=ec15c6093052c02efbd22b6cd&id=57c9ea0469&e=d1c1b9864f)**** Explains how the changes would work if voters approve.

**WHAT IT DOES:**
* **Larger Homestead Exemption:** Increases the amount of your home's value that could be exempt from taxes, potentially lowering your tax bill.
* **Stronger Homeowner Protections:** Updates Save Our Homes protections and helps prevent long-time residents— especially seniors-from being taxed out of their homes.
* **Guardrails on Tax Growth:** Creates additional constitutional limits on how counties and cities can levy and use property tax revenue.
* **Focused on Florida Homeowners:** Protects homesteaded properties and prioritizes long-term Florida residents.

**WHAT HAPPENS NEXT:**

* **Voters Decide In 2026:** Because this is a constitutional amendment, it requires 60% voter approval on the 2026 ballot.
* **Nothing Changes Now:** Current property tax laws remain in place until (and unless) voters approve the proposal.
* **Local Services Continue:** Schools, public safety, roads, and other services will continue. This is property tax relief, not property tax elimination.
* **Implementation Plan In Place** : If approved, CS/HB 3F provides the framework for how the changes will be carried out.

---
| |
# Florida's State Budget Passes
---
| | **The Florida Legislature approved a $114.5 billion budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year.** The budget is **$365 million less than the current year's budget** while continuing to fund Florida's core priorities and essential services.
The budget also **maintains more than $14 billion in reserves,** including $8.6 billion in general revenue reserves, $5.7 billion in the Budget Stabilization Fund, and $250 million dedicated to emergency preparedness and response. These reserves help keep Florida financially strong and prepared for future challenges.
---
|
---
| | **SECURING FUNDING FOR MARION COUNTY** I am proud to share that more than**$4.3 million** in local appropriations were included in the 2026-27 state budget to support projects and organizations throughout Marion County. These investments will help strengthen infrastructure, expand access to community services, and improve quality of life for residents across our district.
---
| |
# Marion County Animal Services Shelter
---
[|
---](https://ryanchamberlin.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=ec15c6093052c02efbd22b6cd&id=afc33cbefc&e=d1c1b9864f)
| | It was a special day for Marion County as we celebrated the **opening of the new Marion County Animal Services shelter.** This facility was huge and accommodates all the animals so well. Thanks to the county for their leadership in making this happen! **This facility means safer conditions, better care for animals, and more opportunities for pets to find their forever homes.**
**Thank you to the County leaders, staff, volunteers, and community members** who never stopped pushing for this project. Marion County continues to show what’s possible when we work together for something bigger than ourselves.
---
| | | | | | | | | | |
---
| |
---
| |
# Ocala Marion County Board of REALTORS®
---
|
---
| | **I really enjoyed my recent meeting with the Ocala Marion County Board of REALTORS®.** We went on a deep dive as to what the elimination and replacement of Property Taxes could look like.
---
| |
# Property Tax Discussion
---
|
---
| | I was so happy to meet with some great people at the Standard Coffee Shop in the Villages to discuss property taxes. _(This is a big priority for me and I am glad to continue to meet and speak to people on my views.)_
---
| |
# Villages Charter High School Graduation
---
|
---
| | A huge congrats to the 250+ students who graduated the **Villages Charter High School,** and all the other students who have graduated this past month!
---
|
---
| |
# Association of Network Marketing Professionals (ANMP) Convention
---
|
---
| | I was honored to be a speaker at the **Annual ANMP** event in Dallas. I think it is so important to speak to independent contractors and entrepreneurs about free enterprise. A Special thanks to Garrett McGrath, Sylvia McGrath, and Gordon Hester for helping make this event happen.
---
|
---
| |
# Thank You Law Enforcement Leaders
---
|
---
| |
I appreciated being able to join **CFO Blaise Ingoglia,** Senator Stan McClain, Sheriff Billy Woods, and local law enforcement leaders in Marion County as **the State of Florida awarded $69,117 to combat illegal immigration enforcement efforts** through the 287(g) program.
**I’m grateful for the men and women in law enforcement who work every day to protect our communities;** the same communities my children and grandchild call home. They make the Great State of Florida is the Safe State of Florida.
Thank you to CFO Ingoglia, Senator McClain, Sheriff Woods, and every officer serving Marion County for your continued dedication and sacrifice
---
|
---
|
---
| | Thank you for your continued support of my leadership in the Florida House! I look forward to sharing with you again soon.
Best regards,
---
|
---
| | | | | | | | | | | | **Ryan Chamberlin****State Representative****District 24**

# Wednesday, June 10, 2026
---|---
**Good Morning!** On [this day in 1940](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGyqyAQxvGn0U5nUYJYUNwmXW57SmaBNTJDICObGN_-jHmFU3__-RXfz83eMKaY7__xQYY_S7GZ9pqImTaLmdeSj6W8cri_YuLjuRWmmO0Ag-pAdQJswJgOK9tgHIRZtGTEpAXoedSyXY3WXqGkkWbwahKktRMX7XGSy8XhQm00JwZKgBAwwtg7P0-j8yF4JPIaGwkUIpet55WYPliXdJQ3bb0vjzaZlflZm_FfM1yb4brve_-NXDlqZWQ6s3NYkbtYO3a13Ux47jGlWNXUSLg_MKavxn_74G2G3wAAAP__6etzrA), the first Lone Star Boys State program was held in Austin with 108 participants. Sponsored by the American Legion, Texas Boys State allows hundreds of teenage boys to learn about and experience representative government every year at the University of Texas. **CLARIFICATION:** We ran a story yesterday about the temporary injunction that allows Texas Tech quarterback Brendan Sorsby to play football this year despite being ruled ineligible by the NCAA for gambling. We said the ruling was issued by "a Lubbock judge" named Ken Curry (as most sources described him). A few readers objected that Ken Curry is not from Lubbock, which is true. We learned that Curry is a [retired judge from Tarrant County](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGOpDAQBNCvMVmPbMPCTEBwCdleeiFq2w30ncdGdrMsf3-a-YWNS1XSqz-f8ydy5LT-xieN8r3kOdFZI4lQmTHJltO15COF9eAo116yEKfZatuD7sHoOSDHa-6aMDodHqah0Qx3o--P9t4129i7sCxm0B_kUZuhC1Y_2s4OrfEf3jnT8Pga073RxuhWtzfnH0PrfAgeifwdVacpsORyk42EvrEu8cpfVG4-P5s4biJ7Ve0vZSdlp_M8bzm1r0zZyecYaSVlp3cRhPwGhQIU5EClKju9vMpOrlAKmKDmUt0FFHllx5HlAo-V4O8RVoJ_lMAfpVyw5aNKThDxhLVgOFAIsFZeEwXACoX2iJ6elETZqSlj2E-OkWs_qE6vT-T4BsjPbv8a7f8AAAD__3KBnSI) who was specifically assigned to this case by the presiding judge of the 9th Administrative Judicial Region, Anna Estevez. It's Curry's first case since 2019. The ruling, however, did come from the [Lubbock County District Court](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0L1uwyAUQOGnwVuiCzj8DAyVKm_p0KWjheHaRiIQmZvEfvsqfYWuZ_iG83Mdrz7lVJYvf0NH-1zHgq-WkQi30Rdaaznm-ihxeaRMx32rhKmMAoQ6gTpxGKNP-Rj7LroJouUdOq4NB2Ol6bvVcewnMdtgIureWwyXiFx4M0H0KhrdJffGQHHgHCTI8xSsllOIMXjEYDzrAWOiup1pRcLdtzkf9YnbOdRbl91KdG9MfjAxMDHs78rE8F1b-8ScsSy4MTE08vRoTAwClLRGGyOl0ho0XGy3uXh_pZxTU5r1sNx8yn86_e_J04nfAAAA___pVXW6).

## Karmelo Anthony Found Guilty of Murder
A Collin County jury on Tuesday found Karmelo Anthony [guilty of murder](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkD2OgzAUhE9jOiP_EAKFi23osu2W6GE_wIqxI_slhNuviPYG285oRvPNz228gQ8-Lt-woaH3nMaIewlIhHmESGuKx5ye0S1PH-h45ETo46iEarlouRSjAx-OsamcmYTrZYVGXjspul53TbWa1qHGRmgJIFHPF6l6rcXFNWg1XlpdeXOWiVYKKYUWup5sf9WTdc4Cou2ANQKdp5RrWpHwDWUOR3phrm3aqmBWokdh-oupgalh3_faTuWkOH2mhk-EqeGUmBrukDcMif_BccoeAn9hdt4Sh2chH_mGZCHMfM6-2MQpg73zDZF4IZgmHxemhiob99h9CL60V9aIZQMfPqPof1e-jPoNAAD__-Q1jQI) in the fatal stabbing of 17-year-old Austin Metcalf at a Frisco ISD track meet, ending a trial that drew national attention and sparked debate over self-defense, race, and school safety. Anthony, now 19, stabbed Metcalf once in the chest during an April 2, 2025, confrontation at Kuykendall Stadium after witnesses said Metcalf told Anthony to leave the Memorial High School team tent. Prosecutors called it a provoked "[sneak attack](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLHOnDAQhJ8GOiPbcIALF2noLm1KtNhrWJ3ByOwdx9tHRHmDv5tiNJrv-_Mcn0CRtvk3rGj5G9K44XlEZMY8wsZL2q6Q3puf3xT52nNipG3UUrdCtkLJ0QPFa2xKbyfpjSrRqq5Xsjd135SLNQ-FqjY9uL7TWqJRwUwPlF4GE_quK8neY7JVUilZy7qanOnqyXnvANH1UDQSPXHKFS_I-IUjxCt9MFcurWW0C_N-FPWvQg-FHs7zrEL6NjfGXSj0cMdCDy_IK8Yk_lMJzgRRRPqgeO8eGA8RMh0uCc7gXmJFZHEwTBNtc5mt30-KkY62Kxo5r0Dx3wH-mbaP1X8DAAD__y-Fhfs)." Defense attorneys argued Anthony acted in a split second of fear and never called him to testify. Jurors heard from dozens of witnesses over [five days of trial](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLHOpCAURp8GOwwgo1hQbGM3225pEC5KFsHAdRzffjOTfYO__pKT75w_z_lpQgxp_W120Pj2eU5w1QiIUGaTcMvp9vlMbj1DxPsoGSGkWTDRU9ZTzmZnQrxn2Ti9MDfyBjQfFGdq7JRsNj2At0J4z-XivR-VN-rheN8z56Xi8GiC_sBYzxnnrGNdu9hx6BbrnDUAVhkiGbiAubS4AcLbVB_v_ILS2rw3UW-IRyXdLyImIqbrutq0WOevz0zE9PEhYorZmkjEZGOuIa3UlPXcIWGl8D7AIjiKJ1RnbhoS_WvKDjHT_wUq3c_ioFAs4UuRrOsGIYmYmqLdcYUYQ-0HItm6mxC_z_BnPV9a_AsAAP__EJmOHw), including students who saw the confrontation and the medical examiner who said the wound pierced Metcalf's heart. The judge allowed jurors to consider a lesser manslaughter charge, but they convicted on murder. The jury sentenced Anthony to 35 years in prison. He will be eligible for parole after half of that time is served.
